results.note: Every number confirmed: eight placebo-controlled trials and 1239 participants (Abstract › Results, p. 1; 3.2, p. 3); 611 in seven bupropion-alone trials at 300 mg/day and 628 in the two stages of Trivedi et al. (3.2, part printed on p. 4); 403 in stage 1 and 225 in stage 2 (Table 1, p. 5), stage 2 being stage-1 placebo non-responders re-randomized (3.2, p. 4; Table 1 footnote e). Editors' 1014 recomputed (611 + 403). Only the locator changes: the search end date (records published to 31 October 2022) is in Abstract › Method, not Abstract › Results. Role qualifies is right.
results.corrected_locator: Abstract › Method and Results (p. 1); 3.2 Characteristics of included studies, 1st paragraph (begins p. 3, continues p. 4); Table 1 and footnote e (p. 5)

results.note: 3.4.1, 1st paragraph (p. 4): 7 reports, 15,664 collected and valid urine samples (one study's positive weeks included), I² about 89%, RR 0.90 (0.84, 0.96), one study at high and three at some concerns of bias, very low GRADE. Table 3 on the rendered p. 7: 7; 15664 urine samples (or weeks); 89%; 0.90 (0.84, 0.96); P < 0.001; low risk 3, some concerns 3, high risk 1; minor asymmetry; very low. Role qualifies is right.

Table 4 on the rendered p. 9: ATS use by UA, 300 mg without naltrexone, N 5 (footnote 1: Das 2010, Elkashef 2008, Heinzerling 2013 and 2014, Shoptaw 2008), RR 0.90 (0.81, 1.00); 450 mg with naltrexone, N 2 (footnote 2: Trivedi 2021), 0.92 (0.89, 0.94); neither row is bold, so no significant subgroup difference (footnote a). Both rows carry the asterisk for an individually significant effect (P < 0.05), so the printed upper limit 1.00 is presumably rounded from just below 1. Editors' sum recomputed from Table 1 (p. 5): 73 + 151 + 30 + 19 + 84 = 357; the page could add p. 5 for that sum.

2.4, 2nd paragraph (p. 3): the overall proportion of positive urine samples or positive weeks per arm was pooled; 2.7.1 (p. 3): dichotomous outcomes pooled as RR and RD by random-effects inverse variance; 3.4.1 (p. 4): 15,664 samples; Table 3 (p. 7): the N column gives 15664 urine samples (or weeks) and 119680 pills (also 3.4.3, p. 6). The editors' reading is labelled and well supported, although the review never states its unit of analysis: Table 4 (p. 9) gives single-trial intervals that person-level data could not produce, e.g. adherence RR 0.94 (0.92, 0.96) in the less-than-daily subgroup, which is one trial (Heinzerling et al., 2013, 19 participants; the other two less-than-daily trials have no adherence data in Table 2), and urine RR 0.80 (0.71, 0.90) in the men-only subgroup (Das et al., 2010, 30 participants).

Table 1 (p. 5): Anderson 2015, 204 participants, the largest of the seven bupropion-alone trials (73, 151, 30, 19, 84, 204, 50); Ghoreishi 2017, 50. Table 2 (p. 6, rendered at 220 dpi): both cells in the ATS-use column are yellow, the colour the legend gives to results unavailable after correspondence with the authors. Consistent with 3.3 (p. 4): main outcome from six studies plus Elkashef's positive weeks.

3.4.2 (begins p. 4, continues p. 6): 7 reports, 786 participants, I² 6%, RR 0.97 (0.89, 1.05), GRADE high (p. 6); 3.4.3 (p. 6): 6 reports, 119,680 pills, I² 99%, RR 0.91 (0.84, 0.99) favouring placebo, GRADE very low; Table 3 (p. 7) agrees. A reporting point outside the anchor: Table 2 (p. 6) marks retention as available for eight reports (both Trivedi stages), but the analysis has seven; 786 equals the six bupropion-alone trials with retention data plus Trivedi stage 2 (561 + 225, editors' calculation from Table 1), and Table 4 lists one 450-mg report for retention, so one Trivedi stage was left out without comment.

Every number confirmed: 344 randomized, 172 per arm (Figure 1, rendered p. 583); 339 received medication, 167 placebo and 172 mirtazapine, all analysed for the primary outcome (Abstract › Results, p. 581; Figure 1; Results › Participants, p. 584); mean age 42.0 (SD 8.6), 126 (37.2%) female (pp. 581, 584). Two elements are not at the stated places: the six Australian outpatient clinics are in Abstract › Design, Setting, and Participants (p. 581) and Methods › Trial Design (p. 582), and the DSM-5 criterion is in Methods › Participants (p. 582); the Abstract says moderate to severe without naming DSM-5. Role supports is right.
results.corrected_locator: Abstract › Design, Setting, and Participants and Results (p. 581); Methods › Trial Design and Participants (p. 582); Figure 1 (p. 583); Results › Participants, 1st paragraph (p. 584)

results.note: Results › Change in Methamphetamine Use, 1st paragraph (p. 585; one paragraph running into the right column): baseline 22.0 (20.3–23.8) and 23.1 (21.3–24.9); change −4.8 and −7.0; estimand −2.2 (−4.2 to −0.2), P = .02; IRR 0.89 (0.80–0.98). Table 2 on the rendered page agrees. Editors' calculation recomputed: 22.0 − 4.8 = 17.2 and 23.1 − 7.0 = 16.1; the IRR equals the ratio of the arms' week-12 to baseline ratios (0.697 / 0.782 = 0.89). For the claim: the week-12 level difference is therefore about 1.1 days, half the 2.2-day difference in change, because the mirtazapine arm started 1.1 days higher.
Same paragraph, right column of p. 585: week 4 −1.3 (−3.3 to 0.6), P = .20; week 8 −1.9 (−3.9 to 0.1), P = .06; mean over the 12-week intervention a reduction of 1.8 days (−3.5 to −0.1), P = .03.

Table 2 on the rendered p. 585: oral fluid 12.0 vs 13.2, estimand 1.3 (−4.7 to 7.2), P = .68; PHQ-9 −0.2 (−1.3 to 1.0), .77; AIS-5 −0.6 (−1.4 to 0.2), .13; HIV risk −0.3 (−1.0 to 0.3), .32; EQ-5D 0.9 (−3.1 to 4.9), .66; Results › Secondary End Points: no significant difference. The anchor rightly does not call the oral-fluid figure a week-12 value: it is an average estimand over weeks 4, 8 and 12 (Methods › End Points, p. 583; Statistical Analysis, p. 584), which the editor may add. The 1.3 is the model estimand; the printed percentages differ by 1.2.

Methods › Participants (p. 582): age 18 to 65, DSM-5 moderate or severe disorder in the past year, use at least twice weekly in the past 4 weeks, positive amphetamine screen; exclusions include prescribed antidepressants, suicide attempt in the past year, and pregnancy or lactation (also acute medical care, inpatient treatment, incarceration, contraindications). Methods › Procedures (p. 582): referral information, harm-reduction brochure, free use of other services. Table 1 (p. 584): PHQ-9 of 10 or more in 82 (49.1) and 83 (48.3). The wording could say pregnancy or lactation.

Methods › Trial Design (p. 582; the paragraph continues into the right column): all clinicians, researchers and investigators blinded to allocation. Methods › End Points, 1st paragraph (p. 583): timeline follow-back primary outcome; in this trial, 89% sensitivity and 83% specificity of the past 3 days of self-report against methamphetamine-positive oral fluid.

Table 3 on the rendered p. 586: all discontinuations 36 (22) vs 49 (28); due to adverse reactions 25 (15) vs 40 (23). Results › Participants, 1st paragraph (p. 584): 85 (25%) and 65 (19%), 23% vs 15%, MEMS median 52% (26%–78%), week-12 data for 293 of 339 (86%). The per-arm counts are in Table 3 (and Figure 1, p. 583) rather than in the paragraph, as the locator allows. Table 3 calls the second row discontinuation due to adverse reactions; the anchor follows the Results' wording (reasons related to the medication).

Table 3 on the rendered p. 586: drowsiness 55 (33) vs 80 (47), P = .01; weight gain 5 (3) vs 17 (10), P = .01; any serious adverse event 11 (7) vs 7 (4). Results › Safety (p. 586): 18 serious adverse events, 7 on mirtazapine, none deemed related to the trial medication.

Author list (p. 581): Steven Shoptaw is second author. Methods › Trial Design (p. 582): phase 3, investigator-led, six government-run outpatient clinics in Australia, coordinated and sponsored by the University of New South Wales. Author Contributions (the section starts on p. 587; the concept-and-design list heads p. 588): Shoptaw listed for concept and design and for critical review. His affiliation (David Geffen School of Medicine, Los Angeles) is under Author Affiliations, p. 587.
